topic: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
title: Capacity and supported decision-making
blurb: Apply the Mental Capacity Act to people with learning disabilities: presume capacity, give real support to decide, assess decision by decision and respect unwise choices.
question: Mohammed, 34, has a moderate learning disability and needs a hernia repair. In a rushed clinic appointment he said 'no', then 'yes', and could not say what the operation involved. The surgeon wants to record that he lacks capacity. What should the learning disability nurse advise?

teach.body: The Mental Capacity Act 2005 (England and Wales, age 16 and over) starts by assuming that every person can make their own decisions. A person lacks capacity only if, at the time, they cannot make a particular decision because of an impairment of, or disturbance in the functioning of, the mind or brain. In plain English: a learning disability tells you nothing on its own. You ask about this decision, now, after giving the person every chance to decide.

teach.h: The five principles in learning disability practice
head: Principle (s1)
In practice
rows: Diagnosis or IQ is never the starting point
Easy read, pictures, signs, right time and place
Only once incapacity for this decision is shown
Choose what limits rights and freedom least

letters.word: Use or Weigh it to decide
Communicate the decision by any means

teach.caption: Failing any one of the four, because of an impairment of mind or brain, means the person lacks capacity for that decision at that time.

teach.h: What the law will not allow
teach.body: Lack of capacity cannot be established merely by reference to a person's age or appearance, or a condition or aspect of behaviour that might lead others to make unjustified assumptions (s2(3)). The impairment may be permanent or temporary (s2(2)), so a learning disability and a short-lived delirium both count, but neither proves incapacity. Capacity is decided on the balance of probabilities (s2(4)).

steps.label: Prepare
steps.sub: Easy read, photos, objects; quiet place; good time of day

steps.label: Involve
steps.sub: Someone who knows how the person communicates

steps.label: Explain
steps.sub: Simple language, visual aids, small chunks (s3(2))

steps.label: Check
steps.sub: Open question: 'tell me what will happen'

steps.label: Time to weigh
steps.sub: Repeat over more than one session if needed

steps.label: Record
steps.sub: Steps taken and how the person decided

teach.h: Details of the test that help people with learning disabilities
teach.body: A person is not unable to understand if they can understand an explanation given in a way appropriate to them, using simple language, visual aids or any other means (s3(2)). Retaining information for a short period is enough (s3(3)). Relevant information includes the reasonably foreseeable consequences of deciding one way or another, or of not deciding (s3(4)). Communicating 'by any means' includes signs, pointing and eye gaze (s3(1)(d)). For sex, the person must understand the other person must be able to consent and must consent throughout (A Local Authority v JB [2021] UKSC 52).

teach.h: Unwise decision or lack of capacity?
teach.caption: s1(4): a person is not to be treated as unable to decide merely because they make an unwise decision.

teach.body: Changing answers in a rushed appointment shows the support was not right, not that Mohammed lacks capacity. The nurse advises that all practicable steps have not been taken. She arranges a second session in a quiet room with an easy read leaflet, photos of the ward, and his sister, who knows his signs. She explains in small chunks, including what happens if he does not have the operation, then asks him to tell her in his own words. He explains and weighs it, and consents.

teach.text: 'Yes' is not understanding: many people with learning disabilities agree to please (acquiescence), so use open questions. And capacity is decision-specific and time-specific: lacking capacity to manage a tenancy says nothing about deciding on a flu vaccine today.

items: Presume capacity; a learning disability alone never shows incapacity (s2(3)).
All practicable steps first: easy read, visual aids, right time, trusted supporter (s1(3), s3(2)).
Test: understand, retain (briefly is enough), use or weigh, communicate by any means.
Information includes consequences of deciding either way or not deciding (s3(4)).
Unwise is not incapable; capacity is decision- and time-specific.

summary: You can now apply the Mental Capacity Act principles and functional test to people with learning disabilities, take all practicable steps to support decision-making, avoid acquiescence traps, and tell an unwise decision from a lack of capacity.

A.q: Which section of the Mental Capacity Act 2005 says a person is not to be regarded as unable to understand if they can understand an explanation given in simple language, with visual aids or any other means?
options: Section 4(6)
Section 3(2)
Section 5
Section 44
A.why: MCA s3(2): a person is not unable to understand if they can understand an explanation given in a way appropriate to their circumstances (simple language, visual aids or any other means).

whyNot.0: s4(6) concerns the person's wishes, feelings, beliefs and values in best interests decisions.
whyNot.2: s5 gives protection for acts done in connection with care or treatment.
whyNot.3: s44 creates the offence of ill-treatment or wilful neglect.

A.q: Carl, 52, has a learning disability and is deciding whether to have a cataract operation. Which information is relevant to his decision under MCA s3(4)?
options: The detailed surgical technique the surgeon will use
What is likely to happen if he decides either way or not at all
Outcome statistics for all cataract operations nationally
His family's views on whether he should have the operation
A.why: s3(4): relevant information includes the reasonably foreseeable consequences of deciding one way or another, or failing to decide.

whyNot.0: Technical detail is not needed; the salient facts and consequences are.
whyNot.2: National statistics are not the core information he needs.
whyNot.3: Family views matter in best interests decisions, not in what Carl must understand.

A.q: A team is uncertain whether Amy, 23, who has a learning disability, has capacity to decide where to live. What standard of proof applies to deciding whether she lacks capacity?
options: Beyond reasonable doubt
Clear and convincing evidence
Agreement of two doctors
The balance of probabilities
A.why: MCA s2(4): any question of whether a person lacks capacity is decided on the balance of probabilities.

whyNot.0: That is the criminal standard, not the MCA standard.
whyNot.1: This is not the standard set by the MCA.
whyNot.2: The MCA does not require two doctors; the decision-maker assesses capacity.

B.q: Sara, 30, has a learning disability and epilepsy. An hour after a seizure she is confused and cannot follow a discussion about a non-urgent change to her medicines. What is the most accurate position?
options: She may lack capacity now, so wait until she recovers
She cannot lack capacity, as confusion after a seizure is short-lived
She lacks capacity for medicine decisions from now on
She has capacity, as she had it before the seizure
B.why: s2(2): the impairment can be temporary. Capacity is time-specific, so a non-urgent decision should wait until she has recovered.

whyNot.1: Temporary disturbances can cause a lack of capacity (s2(2)).
whyNot.2: Capacity is time-specific; post-seizure confusion is temporary.
whyNot.3: Capacity is assessed at the time of the decision, not assumed from before.

B.q: Liam, 24, has a moderate learning disability and wants a sexual relationship with his girlfriend. Following A Local Authority v JB (2021), which information must he be able to understand to have capacity to consent to sex?
options: The legal age for marriage and civil partnership in England
The full sexual history of his girlfriend before they met
That the other person must be able to consent and consent throughout
That relationships need the approval of his family and his staff
B.why: The Supreme Court in JB held that the relevant information includes that the other person must have capacity to consent and must give and maintain consent.

whyNot.0: Marriage law is not part of the test for capacity to consent to sex.
whyNot.1: A partner's history is not part of the relevant information.
whyNot.3: Family or staff approval has no part in his capacity or his rights.

B.q: Wendy, 45, has a learning disability. When the nurse asks about her endoscopy she says 'yes' to every question, including two that contradict each other. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Record that she understands, as she agrees with every point
Record that she lacks capacity, as her answers contradict each other
Use open questions with pictures to check what she understands
Ask her support worker to confirm her consent on her behalf
B.why: Agreeing with everything suggests acquiescence. Open questions, ideally with pictures, check real understanding before any conclusion (s1(3), s3(2)).

whyNot.0: Agreement is not evidence of understanding.
whyNot.1: All practicable steps must be taken before concluding she lacks capacity.
whyNot.3: A support worker cannot consent for an adult.

C.q: Mohammed, 34, has a moderate learning disability and needs a non-urgent hernia repair. In a rushed clinic he said 'no', then 'yes', and could not describe the operation. The surgeon wants to record that he lacks capacity. What should the learning disability nurse advise?
options: Record that he lacks capacity, as his answers kept changing
Accept his final answer of 'yes' as valid consent today
Arrange another session with easy read, photos and his sister
Ask his sister to decide for him in his best interests
C.why: All practicable steps have not been taken (s1(3)). A second session with accessible information and a trusted supporter gives him a real chance to understand and weigh the decision.

whyNot.0: Inconsistent answers in a rushed setting show the support was wrong, not that he lacks capacity.
whyNot.1: He could not describe the operation, so consent is not yet valid.
whyNot.3: His sister holds no legal authority to decide for him, and best interests applies only after incapacity for this decision is shown.

C.q: Gary, 40, has a mild learning disability and has been assessed as having capacity to manage his money. He spends most of his benefits on football memorabilia and runs short of food at the end of each month. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Ask the DWP to make a staff member his appointee
Hold his bank card in the office for safekeeping
Apply to the Court of Protection for a property deputy
Respect his choice and offer budgeting support
C.why: Gary has capacity. s1(4): an unwise decision does not mean a lack of capacity. Staff respect his choice and offer accessible budgeting help.

whyNot.0: An appointee is not appropriate for a person with capacity to manage his own money.
whyNot.1: Taking his card without consent restricts a person who has capacity.
whyNot.2: A deputy is appointed only for someone who lacks capacity.

C.q: On Monday, during a severe chest infection, Ellie, 38, who has a learning disability, was assessed as lacking capacity to decide about moving to a new home. By Friday she has recovered and asks to talk about the move. What should happen?
options: Rely on Monday's assessment for the next twelve months
Reassess, as capacity is time-specific and she has recovered
Continue with the best interests decision already planned
Ask an independent advocate to make the decision for her
C.why: Capacity is time-specific (s2(1) 'at the material time'), and she may have regained it. If she can now decide, it is her decision.

whyNot.0: An assessment applies to the time it was made; her situation has changed.
whyNot.2: Best interests applies only while she lacks capacity.
whyNot.3: An IMCA represents and supports a person; they do not make the decision.

reteach.title: Build the ramp before the test
reteach.question: If a person failed a capacity test because the information came as a dense letter in a noisy room, did they fail, or did we?

blocks.body: The law says you cannot treat someone as unable to decide until all practicable steps to help them have failed. For a person with a learning disability, that means accessible information, the right moment, the right place and the right people. Only then do you ask: can they understand, retain, weigh and communicate?

blocks.text: Retaining information for a short time is enough (s3(3)). Forgetting the next day does not mean a person lacked capacity at the time.

explain.body: Everyone 16 and over is presumed to have capacity (s1(2)). A condition such as a learning disability cannot by itself establish a lack of capacity (s2(3)).

test.q: Patrice, 27, has a moderate learning disability and says she does not want a flu vaccine. The practice nurse says, 'She has a learning disability, so I'll ask her mum instead.' What is the most appropriate response?
options: Agree, and record the mother's consent in the notes
Presume Patrice has capacity and support her to decide
Give the vaccine now under a best interests decision
Agree, as a moderate learning disability means incapacity
test.why: s1(2) and s2(3): capacity is presumed and cannot be established merely by reference to a condition. Patrice is supported to make her own decision.

whyNot.0: A parent cannot consent for an adult without legal authority.
whyNot.2: Best interests applies only after incapacity for the decision is shown.
whyNot.3: No level of learning disability establishes incapacity by itself.

explain.body: Easy read, pictures, objects, signs, a quiet place, the best time of day, someone who knows the person's communication, more than one session. Explanations in simple language or with visual aids are required before concluding someone cannot understand (s3(2)).

test.q: Rosa, 44, has a moderate learning disability and is invited for cervical screening. Her capacity to decide is in doubt. Which step should come before any assessment?
options: Explain with pictures and someone who knows her
Ask her to sign after a verbal explanation
Post her the standard invitation leaflet again
Book a shorter appointment to reduce her worry
test.why: s1(3): all practicable steps to help her decide must be taken, including accessible information and her usual communication supports.

whyNot.1: A verbal explanation alone may not be accessible to Rosa.
whyNot.2: The standard leaflet is the format that has not worked.
whyNot.3: A shorter appointment gives less time to understand, not more.

explain.body: Understand, retain (briefly is enough), use or weigh, and communicate by any means, including signs and eye pointing.

test.q: Hollie, 31, has a learning disability. In a session about a knee injection she understands and weighs the information and decides, but a week later cannot recall the discussion. Does this prevent her having had capacity?
options: Yes, she must remember it until the injection
Yes, poor recall shows she could not weigh it
No, as she retained it for at least a day
No, retaining it long enough to decide is enough
test.why: s3(3): being able to retain information for a short period only does not prevent a person being regarded as able to decide.

whyNot.0: The Act does not require retention until the procedure.
whyNot.1: She did weigh it at the time.
whyNot.2: The Act sets no minimum period such as a day; long enough to decide is the test.

explain.body: A person with capacity can make choices others think unwise (s1(4)). Keep offering accessible information and support; do not override the decision.

test.q: Dean, 35, has a mild learning disability and asthma. He has capacity to decide about smoking and chooses to carry on despite clear, accessible advice. What should the nurse do?
options: Reassess his capacity, as this choice is unwise
Respect his choice and keep offering stop-smoking support
Ask staff to hold his cigarettes and ration them daily
Make a best interests plan to reduce his smoking
test.why: s1(4): an unwise decision does not mean a lack of capacity. Dean's choice stands; support to stop continues in an accessible way.

whyNot.0: An unwise choice by itself is not a reason to doubt capacity.
whyNot.2: Restricting a person with capacity is not lawful without consent.
whyNot.3: Best interests does not apply when he has capacity.
